question: When are source-code comments worth writing, and which kinds are harmful?
hypothesis: Comments compensate for failure to express intent in code, so they should be minimised and the code made expressive instead.
contributions: A catalogue of 8 kinds of good comment and about 22 kinds of bad comment, with examples from FitNesse, Tomcat, JCommon and Apache Commons
A before/after refactoring of a prime generator (Listings 4-7, 4-8)

results.claim: Martin states outright that comments are always failures: they exist to compensate for failing to express intent in code.
results.setup: Opening argument of the chapter, no data; printed page 54 (PDF page 2), second paragraph.
results.note: Same paragraph: 'The proper use of comments is to compensate for our failure to express ourself in code.' The sentence is in this chapter on printed p. 54. On p. 53 he calls comments 'at best, a necessary evil'. The following sentence concedes 'We must have them because we cannot always figure out how to express ourselves without them'.

results.claim: Comments are called a necessary evil, not pure good, at the chapter's opening.
results.setup: Printed p. 53; premise is that sufficiently expressive languages would remove most need for comments.
results.quote: comments are, at best, a necessary evil.

results.claim: Why he dislikes comments: they go stale, more so the older they are and the farther from the code.
results.setup: p. 54; illustrated with the HTTP_DATE_REGEXP comment orphaned by later-added instance variables.
results.quote: Why am I so down on comments? Because they lie.

results.claim: An inaccurate comment is worse than none; the code is the only reliable source of truth.
results.quote: Inaccurate comments are far worse than no comments at all.
results.note: Next paragraph: 'Truth can only be found in one place: the code.'

results.claim: The only truly good comment is the one you found a way not to write.
results.quote: the only truly good comment is the comment you found a way not to write.

results.claim: Comments do not make up for bad code; clean the code instead.
results.quote: Clear and expressive code with few comments is far superior to cluttered and complex code with lots of comments.

results.claim: Replace a comment with a well-named function (employee.isEligibleForFullBenefits()).
results.quote: In many cases it’s simply a matter of creating a function that says the same thing as the comment you want to write.

results.claim: In the refactored prime generator he keeps two comments; the sqrt-limit rationale is 'almost certainly necessary' because no name or structure could express it.
results.quote: There are just two comments in the whole module.
results.note: He also doubts the sqrt optimisation itself may be worth the reader effort.

limits: No empirical evidence: all positions are the author's experience and opinion, with Java examples from 2000s open-source code.

The chapter allows 8 good kinds (legal, informative, intent, clarification, warning of consequences, TODO, amplification, public-API javadocs), so 'always failures' is paired with explicit concessions.
Does not contain the Ousterhout exchange (the 10-100x cost claim, 5-10x more comments) or any Martin reply; those are from the later debate, not this chapter.
Some advice has dated: @Ignore replaces underscore-disabled tests (said in the text), IDE TODO search and spell check exist.
practices: Do not comment bad code; rewrite it (epigraph from Kernighan and Plauger, p. 53).
Before writing a comment, try to express the intent in code, with a function or variable name (pp. 54-55, 67).
Keep comments for legal headers, intent or rationale, warnings of consequences, amplification, and public API javadocs (pp. 55-59).
Prefer renaming (responderBeingTested) over an informative comment (p. 56).
Take extra care that clarifying comments are correct (p. 57).
Scan TODOs regularly and remove those you can; a TODO is not an excuse for bad code (p. 59).
Delete commented-out code; source control remembers it (p. 69).
Remove journal, byline and attribution comments; source control records them (pp. 63-64, 68).
Do not put system-wide information (such as a default port) in a local comment (pp. 69-70).
Avoid closing-brace comments; shorten the function instead (p. 67).
Do not mandate a javadoc for every function or variable (p. 63).
Do not write javadocs for non-public code (p. 71).

terms.definition: Comments that restate the obvious and provide no new information.
Plopping in a comment just because you feel you should or because the process requires it.
A comment required by a rule that every function or variable have one.
A change log accumulated at the start of a module on every edit.
A comment describing a distant part of the system, not the code beside it.
